subject: community-medicine
title: Nutritional Protein Quality: Biological Value and Amino Acid Scores

steps.title: Protein quality versus quantity in human nutrition
steps.tx: In community nutritional assessment, evaluating dietary protein requires analyzing both total quantity and intrinsic quality, which dictates how efficiently ingested nitrogen is retained for tissue synthesis and maintenance. While animal proteins from eggs and milk supply all nine essential amino acids in optimal proportions, cereal-heavy vegetarian diets often contain lower protein densities that demand careful biochemical evaluation of **protein nutritional quality**.
steps.say: Total protein intake matters, but biological quality is what determines how well the body uses it for growth and tissue repair. Vegetarian diets require careful evaluation of protein quality.

right.title: Incomplete plant proteins (cereals, pulses)
points: Lacks one or more essential amino acids
Lower digestibility due to phytates and fibre

steps.title: Biological value: retained nitrogen proportion
steps.tx: The classical physiological index of protein quality is the **biological value calculation**, defined as the percentage of absorbed nitrogen that is retained by the body for growth and cellular maintenance. Experimentally measured using nitrogen balance studies in human volunteers, whole hen egg protein achieves a biological value of roughly ninety-six to one hundred, serving as the biological reference standard against which all other dietary proteins are judged.
steps.say: Biological value measures the percentage of absorbed nitrogen that the body retains for repair. Whole egg sets the international gold standard with a biological value near one hundred.

steps.title: Digestibility coefficient and nitrogen absorption
steps.tx: Before protein nitrogen can be utilized for protein synthesis, it must be hydrolyzed by gastrointestinal enzymes and absorbed across the enterocyte brush border, measured as the **digestibility coefficient calculation**. Expressed as absorbed nitrogen divided by total ingested food nitrogen times one hundred, animal proteins demonstrate digestibility exceeding ninety-five percent, whereas plant grains average seventy-five to eighty-five percent due to indigestible cell wall fibres and phytates.
steps.say: The digestibility coefficient is the percentage of eaten protein that the gut actually absorbs into the bloodstream. Plant proteins are absorbed less efficiently because plant fibres trap nutrients.

steps.title: Net protein utilisation: integrating absorption and retention
steps.tx: To capture both digestibility and subsequent physiological retention in a single comprehensive metric, nutritionists calculate **net protein utilisation**. Computed mathematically as biological value multiplied by the digestibility coefficient divided by one hundred, it directly measures the percentage of ingested dietary nitrogen that is retained by the body; whole egg yields an index around ninety to ninety-five, while polished rice averages fifty-five to sixty.
steps.say: Net protein utilisation multiplies biological value by digestibility. It reveals the exact percentage of eaten protein that the body keeps for growth and tissue repair.

nodes.label: Percentage of eaten protein retained by body

steps.title: Amino acid score and provisional reference pattern
steps.tx: At the molecular level, nutritional chemists evaluate food proteins using the **amino acid score calculation**, also termed chemical score. The concentration of each essential amino acid in one gram of test protein is expressed as a percentage of the concentration of the same amino acid in an ideal provisional reference pattern established by the FAO and WHO, with whole egg or human milk serving as reference profiles.
steps.say: The amino acid score compares each essential amino acid in a food against an ideal pattern set by the World Health Organization. It reveals exactly which amino acids fall short.

left.title: Amino acid chemical score
points: (mg of amino acid in 1 g test protein / mg in reference) x 100
Does not account for digestive losses in the gut

right.title: PDCAAS (Digestibility corrected)
points: Amino acid score multiplied by faecal digestibility
Modern regulatory standard for nutrition labeling
Truncated at a maximum score of 1.0

steps.title: Limiting amino acids in staple grains
steps.tx: In any incomplete plant protein, the specific essential amino acid showing the lowest chemical percentage relative to the reference standard is designated the **limiting amino acid**. Because protein synthesis ceases as soon as any single essential building block is exhausted, the limiting amino acid dictates overall biological value; in cereals such as wheat, rice and maize, lysine is limiting, whereas in pulses, methionine and cysteine are limiting.
steps.say: The limiting amino acid is the essential amino acid present in the smallest amount relative to need. In wheat and rice, lysine is limiting; in lentils and pulses, methionine is limiting.

steps.title: Mutual supplementation in Indian traditional diets
steps.tx: Traditional Indian culinary practices intuitively overcome plant amino acid deficits through **mutual dietary supplementation**, combining cereals and pulses in a single meal. Because cereals are rich in sulfur amino acids (methionine) but poor in lysine, while pulses are rich in lysine but poor in methionine, eating rice with dal or roti with lentils in a four to one ratio achieves an amino acid score rivaling animal protein.
steps.say: Eating rice and dal or roti and lentils together creates a complete protein. The excess methionine in rice covers the deficit in dal, while the lysine in dal fixes the deficit in rice.

nodes.label: Cereals: Rich in methionine, poor in lysine
Pulses: Rich in lysine, poor in methionine

steps.title: Protein-energy ratio in community diets
steps.tx: To determine whether a community diet supplies adequate protein density to support child growth, nutritionists calculate the **protein-energy percentage ratio**, expressing energy derived from protein as a percentage of total daily dietary calories. For healthy adults, protein should contribute ten to fifteen percent of total energy, while pregnant women and convalescing children require ratios approaching twelve to fifteen percent to support rapid lean tissue deposition.
steps.say: Protein should supply ten to fifteen percent of your daily calories. Growing children and pregnant mothers require the higher end of this range to build new muscle and organs.

rows: Easily met by balanced cereal-pulse diet
Requires extra pulse, milk or egg portions

steps.title: Protein quality in Supplementary Nutrition programs
steps.tx: National supplementary feeding programs, including the Integrated Child Development Services and PM POSHAN school lunches, mandate strict **supplementary nutrition standards** to safeguard growing children. Hot cooked meals must provide at least four hundred and fifty to five hundred kilocalories and twelve to fifteen grams of protein for primary schoolchildren, combining sprouted legumes, groundnuts, fortified millets and eggs to ensure high biological value.
steps.say: School lunch programmes mandate hot meals providing five hundred calories and fifteen grams of high-quality protein, using lentils, fortified grains and eggs to support child growth.

nodes.label: Use of sprouted pulses, millets and eggs
Prevention of stunting, wasting and anaemia
